title: Products of Brown localizations
statement:
Use quasicategories, nerves and coherent functor categories of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], in universes enlarged to contain all categories and mapping spaces in question. Let $J$ be any small set. For each $j\in J$ let $\mathcal A_j$ be an ordinary category with initial object $0_j$ and classes $C_j,W_j$ containing isomorphisms and closed under composition. Assume $W_j$ has two-out-of-three and is retract closed, every $0_j\to X$ belongs to $C_j$, every arrow factors as a member of $C_j$ followed by a member of $W_j$, pushouts of members of $C_j$ exist and belong to $C_j$, and pushouts of members of $C_j\cap W_j$ belong to $C_j\cap W_j$. Write $q_j:N(\mathcal A_j)\to L_j$ for a homotopy coherent localization, meaning that restriction into any quasicategory identifies the whole functor category out of $L_j$ with the full subcategory inverting $W_j$. Then the functor
$$N(\prod_{j\in J}\mathcal A_j)=\prod_{j\in J}N(\mathcal A_j)\xrightarrow{\prod_jq_j}\prod_{j\in J}L_j$$
is a homotopy coherent localization at the class of coordinatewise weak equivalences. Thus its restriction functor has that same entire-functor-category universal property. The empty product is included. No coproducts in the categories $\mathcal A_j$, no model structures and no finiteness of $J$ are assumed.

source.place: Dual of Proposition 7.7.1, printed p. 396 (PDF p. 411), using the ordinary all-cofibrant case of Definition 7.4.12. No Stacks tag states this arbitrary-product infinity-localization comparison. Read online on 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/.

proof.text: If $J=\varnothing$, both products are terminal simplicial sets and the displayed map is the identity. Restriction along an identity is the identity on every functor category, so the required localization property holds. For arbitrary $J$, put $\mathcal A=\prod_j\mathcal A_j$ and define $C,W$ coordinatewise. Its initial object is $(0_j)$. Composition, isomorphisms, retracts and two-out-of-three are checked in each coordinate. Choose the stated factorization in every coordinate to factor an arrow of $\mathcal A$. For a pushout along $(c_j)\in C$, take the pushouts in every $\mathcal A_j$: giving a map from their tuple is exactly giving compatible maps in each coordinate, so this is a pushout. Its new leg lies in $C$, and in $C\cap W$ if the old leg does, by the hypotheses. Thus $\mathcal A$ has the same all-cofibrant Brown axioms. These simultaneous choices use ordinary choice on the small indexing set, not a functorial factorization or coproducts within any $\mathcal A_j$.

Apply [lem-coef-brown-fibrant-localization-pullbacks] to $\mathcal A^{op}$ with fibrations $C^{op}$ and weak equivalences $W^{op}$, and likewise to each $\mathcal A_j^{op}$. Its terminal, pullback and weak-equivalence/fibration factorization assumptions are exactly the opposites of the axioms just verified. Taking opposites gives a localization $q:N\mathcal A\to L$ with finite coherent colimits, carrying $0$ and cofibration pushouts to initial objects and pushouts. It gives the same assertions for the given $q_j:N\mathcal A_j\to L_j$: two entire-functor-category localizations are equivalent by factoring each through the other and using full faithfulness to identify the composites with the identities. Taking opposites respects localization because $\operatorname{Fun}(U^{op},V)\cong\operatorname{Fun}(U,V^{op})^{op}$, and this identification also takes the full subcategories inverting the specified arrows to each other. Equivalences preserve these cones because the induced maps on mapping spaces are equivalences by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]; apply the mapping-space characterization of a limiting cone and its dual to the quasi-inverse.

source.place: Theorem 7.5.18 and Corollary 7.5.20, dualized; Definition 7.1.2 for uniqueness and opposites

proof.text: Set $\mathcal P=\prod_j L_j$. It is a quasicategory by choosing each inner-horn filler coordinatewise. Internal homs, right-pinched mapping spaces and the comma cocone construction in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones] commute with this product by their displayed degreewise formulas. For a finite coherent diagram into $\mathcal P$, choose a colimiting cocone in each $L_j$. Its tuple is colimiting: the mapping space from this tuple cocone to any cocone is the product of the corresponding contractible Kan mapping spaces. To check contractibility of this possibly infinite product, each map from a factor to the point is a trivial Kan fibration, hence lifts every boundary inclusion by [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]; choose these fillers coordinatewise. The product therefore also lifts all boundary inclusions, including dimension zero, and is a trivial Kan fibration to the point. Kan properties of the cocone mapping spaces are supplied by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. This proves that $\mathcal P$ has finite coherent colimits and that the product of the initial objects or cofibration pushout cocones in step 2 is again an initial object or pushout cocone.

source.place: Proposition 7.7.1, exactness of the product of localization functors; elementary coordinatewise cone calculation

proof.text: The functor $T=\prod_jq_j:N\mathcal A\to\mathcal P$ inverts $W$, since inverses and their two triangle simplices can be chosen coordinatewise. Its localization factorization is $F:L\to\mathcal P$ with a specified coherent equivalence $Fq\simeq T$. Steps 2 and 3 show that $T$ preserves the initial object and every pushout along $C$. All the hypotheses of [lem-coef-brown-right-exact-extension] now hold for $\mathcal A,L,\mathcal P,T$, so $F$ preserves finite coherent colimits.

We prove $F$ conservative without assuming any $W_j$ saturated. By essential surjectivity and left fractions in [lem-coef-brown-left-fractions] for $\mathcal A$, it suffices to consider $\alpha=[q(s)]^{-1}[q(f)]$ from $qX$ to $qY$, where $f:X\to Z$ and $s:Y\to Z$ lies in $C\cap W$. If $F(\alpha)$ is invertible, every $q_j(f_j)$ is invertible. The localized-retraction clause of that same node gives $k_j:Z_j\to U_j$ in $C_j$ with $k_jf_j\in W_j$. Then $q_j(k_j)$ is invertible, so a second application gives $l_j:U_j\to V_j$ in $C_j$ with $l_jk_j\in W_j$. Assemble $k,l$ in $\mathcal A$. The maps $q(kf)$ and $q(lk)$ are invertible, since their strict maps belong to $W$. In $hL$, $q(k)$ has right inverse $q(f)q(kf)^{-1}$ and left inverse $q(lk)^{-1}q(l)$; these inverses coincide by multiplying their defining equations. Thus $q(k)$ and then $q(f)$ are invertible. So is $\alpha$. An edge of a quasicategory is an equivalence exactly when its homotopy-category class is invertible: choose an edge representing the inverse class, represent the two composite equalities by paths to the identity in the Kan mapping spaces, and use inner-horn fillers to insert these homotopies into the composition triangles, obtaining the two inverse-triangle witnesses of the definition. This proves conservativity for every edge, after conjugating its endpoints by equivalences to objects in $q\mathcal A$.

source.place: Proposition 7.7.1, conservativity argument using the dual of Corollary 7.5.19 and left fractions

proof.text: We verify left App 2 for $F$. First take an arrow $\psi:T(X)\to y$ in $\mathcal P$. For each $j$, essential surjectivity in [lem-coef-brown-left-fractions] supplies an equivalence $a_j:y_j\to q_jY_j$. Represent $[a_j\psi_j]$ as $[q_j(s_j)]^{-1}[q_j(f_j)]$ with $f_j:X_j\to Z_j$ and $s_j:Y_j\to Z_j$ in $C_j\cap W_j$. Put $Z=(Z_j)$, $f=(f_j)$ and $e_j=q_j(s_j)a_j$. Each $e_j$ is an equivalence and $[q_j(f_j)]=[e_j\psi_j]$. These equalities assemble into an equality in $h\mathcal P$: in each coordinate Kan mapping space, compose and reverse a finite edge path using horn fillers to obtain one edge between the two representatives, and take the tuple of those edges. No common bound on the lengths of the original coordinate edge paths is required. Consequently $T(f)$ equals $e\psi$ there for $e=(e_j):y\to T(Z)$. For an arbitrary $x\in L$, choose an equivalence $a:x\to qX$ using the same node. Write $\theta:Fq\simeq T$ for the specified coherent equivalence and set $b=\theta_X F(a):F(x)\to T(X)$. Given $\psi:F(x)\to y$, apply the construction to $\psi b^{-1}$, obtaining $f:X\to Z$ and an equivalence $e_T:y\to T(Z)$ with $[T(f)]=[e_T\psi b^{-1}]$. Set $u=q(f)a$ and $e=\theta_Z^{-1}e_T:y\to F(qZ)$. Naturality of $\theta$ gives, in $h\mathcal P$, $[F(u)]=[\theta_Z^{-1}T(f)\theta_XF(a)]=[\theta_Z^{-1}e_T\psi b^{-1}b]=[e\psi]$. Thus the approximation property holds for all objects and arrows, with the comparison components and their directions specified.

source.place: Proposition 7.7.1, App 2 argument; Example 7.6.4 and Definition 7.6.1, dualized

proof.text: The source $L$ and target $\mathcal P$ have finite coherent colimits by steps 2 and 3; $F$ preserves them by step 4, is conservative by step 5 and satisfies left App 2 by step 6. Hence [lem-coef-finite-colimit-approximation] makes $F$ an equivalence of quasicategories. For any quasicategory $\mathcal D$, precomposition with $F$ is an equivalence $\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal P,\mathcal D)\simeq\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal D)$: precomposition with a coherent quasi-inverse supplies its inverse and the unit and counit. Composing with $q^*$ identifies this entire functor category with the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(N\mathcal A,\mathcal D)$ inverting $W$. Under $Fq\simeq T$, this composite is precisely restriction along $\prod_jq_j$. Finally $N\mathcal A=\prod_jN\mathcal A_j$ degreewise because a functor $[n]\to\prod_j\mathcal A_j$ is exactly a tuple of such functors. This is the claimed localization with its specified restriction functor.
